subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric UTI, Reflux, and Uropathology: MCUG, DMSA, and PUV

steps.tx: Bacterial colonization of the urinary tract represents one of the most common serious occult bacterial infections in young febrile infants. In children presenting with unexplained fever, **pediatric urinary tract infection** is predominantly caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli, responsible for eighty percent of episodes. In infants under two years, non-specific symptoms such as irritability, vomiting, poor feeding, failure to thrive, and prolonged neonatal jaundice frequently predominate over localized dysuria.
steps.say: Unexplained fever in an infant is a urinary tract infection until proven otherwise. Escherichia coli is the culprit pathogen in eighty percent of pediatric cases.

steps.tx: Retrograde regurgitation of infected bladder urine into the upper urinary tract predisposes children to recurrent pyelonephritis and parenchymal renal scarring. Classified under the International Reflux Study, **vesicoureteric reflux grading** categorizes severity from Grade I, where urine refluxes into the non-dilated ureter only, to Grade V, characterized by massive tortuous ureteral dilatation, gross hydronephrosis, and complete loss of renal papillary calyceal architecture.
steps.say: Vesicoureteric reflux is graded from one to five based on ureteral dilatation and calyceal blunting. High-grade reflux carries an elevated risk of renal scarring.

rows: Reflux into ureter only; no dilatation
Reflux into ureter, pelvis, and calyces
Normal calyces without blunting or dilatation
Mild to moderate ureteral and pelvic dilatation
Severe tortuous dilatation of ureter and pelvis
Endoscopic Deflux injection or ureteric reimplantation

steps.tx: Fluoroscopic visualization of the lower urinary tract during bladder filling and active voiding provides the definitive diagnostic investigation for anatomical reflux. Performing a **micturating cystourethrogram in children** (MCUG or VCUG) detects the exact grade of vesicoureteric reflux, evaluates bladder diverticula, and identifies obstructing urethral lesions. It is performed after sterile urine is confirmed following acute infection under prophylactic antibiotic cover.
steps.say: A micturating cystourethrogram is the definitive test for grading vesicoureteric reflux and diagnosing urethral valves. Perform it once the acute infection has resolved.

left.title: MCUG Technical Protocol
points: Catheterize bladder under strict aseptic precautions
Instil warm radiopaque contrast under gravity
Capture fluoroscopic images during active voiding
Document reflux grading and urethral anatomy

right.title: Clinical Indications for MCUG
points: Infants under 1 year with confirmed first febrile UTI
Recurrent childhood febrile urinary tract infections
Abnormal renal ultrasound showing hydroureteronephrosis
Male infants with suspected posterior urethral valves

steps.tx: Nuclear renal cortical scintigraphy evaluates acute parenchymal inflammatory defects and permanent focal cortical scarring. Utilizing Technetium-99m dimercaptosuccinic acid, a **DMSA renal cortical scan** represents the gold standard imaging modality for documenting renal parenchymal injury. Performed during acute infection, it shows focal photopenic areas of pyelonephritis, while scans repeated four to six months later document irreversible permanent cortical scars.
steps.say: A DMSA renal cortical scan is the gold standard for detecting pyelonephritis and renal scarring. Scans repeated six months after infection confirm permanent damage.

left.title: Acute Pyelonephritis Phase
points: Performed within 48 to 72 hours of acute fever
Focal photopenic cold areas in renal cortex
Normal kidney outline without loss of volume
Reflects acute tubular ischaemia and inflammation

right.title: Chronic Renal Scarring Phase
points: Performed 4 to 6 months after acute UTI episode
Focal cortical thinning and parenchymal volume loss
Wedged cortical defects with deformed outline
Predisposes to hypertension and chronic kidney disease

steps.tx: Congenital obstructing mucosal folds within the prostatic urethra constitute the most frequent cause of lower urinary tract obstruction in infant males. Characteristically diagnosed in male neonates, **posterior urethral valves** (PUV) arise from persistent embryological folds at the verumontanum. Obstruction produces a poor dribbling urinary stream, a palpable distended bladder, severe bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, oligohydramnios sequence with secondary pulmonary hypoplasia, and early renal dysplasia.
steps.say: Posterior urethral valves are the commonest cause of male infant urinary obstruction. They cause a poor stream, distended bladder, bilateral hydronephrosis, and renal failure.

steps.tx: Intrinsic narrowing at the junction between the renal pelvis and proximal ureter represents the most common cause of congenital hydronephrosis. Often detected on antenatal ultrasound screening, **pelviureteric junction obstruction** (PUJO) results from deficient circular muscular continuity at the renal pelvic outlet. Affected infants demonstrate progressive pelvicalyceal dilatation without ureteral dilatation, which can lead to progressive parenchymal thinning and recurrent flank pain.
steps.say: Pelviureteric junction obstruction causes congenital hydronephrosis without ureteral enlargement. Dynamic diuretic renal scans confirm significant outflow obstruction.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic illustrating obstructive sites including pelviureteric junction obstruction and hydronephrosis.
vis.caption: Sites of urinary tract obstruction showing localized narrowing at the pelviureteric junction. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Standardized ultrasound grading frameworks classify the severity of renal collecting system dilatation in neonates and infants. Evaluating **pelvicalyceal hydronephrosis grading** under the Society for Fetal Urology (SFU) system categorizes kidneys from Grade 0 (normal) to Grade IV, defined by severe pelvicalyceal ballooning and diffuse renal parenchymal thinning. Postnatal ultrasound performed at three to seven days of life guides definitive functional radionuclide testing.
steps.say: The Society for Fetal Urology grades hydronephrosis from zero to four based on caliectasis and parenchymal thickness. Grade four demonstrates severe thinning of the renal cortex.

rows: Uniform dilatation of all major and minor calyces
Severe ballooning of pelvis and calyces

steps.tx: Dynamic diuretic radionuclide scintigraphy quantifies individual renal split function and differentiates mechanical obstruction from passive non-obstructive dilatation. Utilizing Technetium-99m MAG3 or DTPA with intravenous furosemide, **diuretic renal scintigraphy** generates washout curves where an excretion half-time (T-half) exceeding twenty minutes confirms mechanical obstruction. Anderson-Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty provides definitive surgical correction, restoring unobstructed dependent drainage.
steps.say: A diuretic washout half-time over twenty minutes confirms true mechanical obstruction. Anderson-Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty provides definitive surgical cure.

left.title: Diuretic Renogram Interpretation
points: T-half <10 minutes: normal, non-obstructed drainage
T-half 10-20 minutes: equivocal or partial delay
T-half >20 minutes: definitive mechanical obstruction
Split renal function <40% indicates parenchymal compromise

right.title: Anderson-Hynes Pyeloplasty
points: Excision of the stenotic pelviureteric segment
Reduction and tailoring of dilated redundant pelvis
Dismembered spatulated anastomosis over double-J stent
High surgical success rate exceeding 95 percent
